keyVerseText: Beerah his son, whom Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria carried away captive: he was prince of the Reubenites. Tilgathpilneser: or, Tig-lath-pilne-ser, 2.kin.15.29.and 16.7.
rootMeaning: The root of בְּאֵרָה (Bᵉʼêrâh) is בְּאֵרָא (Bᵉʼêrâʼ), which means "a well." This root conveys the idea of a source of water, life, and sustenance, which is fundamental in the arid regions of ancient Israel. The literal sense of "well" enriches the understanding of the name beyond a mere proper noun, suggesting provision and vitality inherent in the name bearer.
usageInScripture: The word בְּאֵרָה appears only once in Scripture, specifically as a proper name, Beerah, identified as a Reubenite chief who was exiled to Assyria. Its consistent translation as a proper name rather than a common noun highlights its unique personal identity rather than a generic object. This singular occurrence emphasizes the historical and genealogical record over a broader lexical range.
theologicalSignificance: Though בְּאֵרָה is primarily a proper name, its root meaning as "well" carries rich theological symbolism. Wells in Scripture often represent God's provision, sustenance, and covenant faithfulness to His people. Recognizing that Beerah's name connects to this imagery invites reflection on God's sustaining presence even amid exile and captivity. It reminds believers that God’s life-giving provision extends through individuals and history, even in times of judgment and displacement.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Chronicles 5:6 notes that Beerah, a prince of the Reubenites, was taken captive by the Assyrian king Tilgathpilneser. The use of בְּאֵרָה here as a personal name grounds this historical event in the lineage of Israel. The name's root meaning, "well," subtly underscores the tragic irony that a bearer of life-giving provision was led away into exile, inviting believers to trust in God’s ultimate restoration beyond such trials.
